data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Decentralized networks are more resilient to correlated failure only when their independence is actively maintained by causal firebreaks (independent codebases, distinct power domains, separate supply chains); without those firebreaks, the apparent diversity masks shared dependencies and the large redundant service is strictly more resilient.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the decentralized nodes converge on a single dominant software implementation (monoculture), a shared defect propagates equally to both topologies.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the large centralized service has logically isolated internal sub-services with independent codebases and teams, it may match or exceed the resilience of the decentralized network.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If independent operators share critical upstream dependencies (e.g., a ubiquitous cloud provider, a compromised common dependency), the decentralized network fails to provide superior correlated failure resistance.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"True resilience to correlated failure is a function of causal independence, not redundancy. Independent codebases, power grids, and teams decouple triggering conditions, preventing the cascading step where a single latent defect propagates through all components simultaneously. In a large centralized service, all redundant components share the same codebase, configuration, and potentially upstream dependencies, meaning a single bug or credential compromise collapses all redundancy at once. The decentralized network provides true redundancy only if its operational diversity introduces genuine causal firebreaks between failure domains.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
